sentences: Kim Hong-do, the leading painter of late Joseon Korea, fit an entire market-day wrestling match onto a single album leaf no bigger than a sheet of paper.
He left the background empty and arranged the spectators in a ring, so your eye drops straight to the two wrestlers locked at the center.
Yet the drama is easiest to read in the crowd: some lean back in surprise, some gape, some hug their knees and hold their breath.
Only the young taffy seller turns away, uninterested.
With a handful of quick brushstrokes, Kim captures not just a scene but its noise and heat.
That is the genius of Danwon's genre painting.
